lem-ip-bpdn-objectives-proper-closed-con.1.1: The function $f$ is finite everywhere because it is a finite sum of absolute values, and $f(0)=0$, so its effective domain is nonempty. For $0\le\theta\le1$, the triangle inequality and homogeneity in [F1] give $f((1-\theta)x+\theta z)\le f((1-\theta)x)+f(\theta z)=(1-\theta)f(x)+\theta f(z).$ Thus $f$ is proper and convex by [F2,F3]. [given, F1, F2, F3, algebra]
lem-ip-bpdn-objectives-proper-closed-con.1.2: For $(x,t)\in\mathbb R^{n+1}$ outside $\operatorname{epi}f$, the gap $d=f(x)-t$ is positive. Put $L=\sqrt{n}+1>0$. If $(x',t')$ has product Euclidean distance $D<d/(2L)$ from $(x,t)$, then coordinate-square domination gives $\|x'-x\|_2\le D$ and $|t'-t|\le D$. By [F1], $f(x')-t'\ge f(x)-t-|f(x')-f(x)|-|t'-t|\ge d-(\sqrt{n}+1)D>d/2>0.$ So the complement of $\operatorname{epi}f$ is open and its epigraph is closed. The scalar $L$ is positive by [F8]; the coordinate-square domination follows by comparing a partial sum with the full nonnegative sum and using [F9]. [given, F1, F6, F7, F8, F9, construct, algebra]
lem-ip-bpdn-objectives-proper-closed-con.1.3: The residual ball $C$ contains $y$ because $\epsilon\ge0$. If $u,v\in C$ and $0\le\theta\le1$, homogeneity and the triangle inequality in [F1] give $\|(1-\theta)u+\theta v-y\|_2\le(1-\theta)\|u-y\|_2+\theta\|v-y\|_2\le\epsilon,$ so $C$ is convex. If $u\notin C$, the gap $d=\|u-y\|_2-\epsilon>0$ and the reverse triangle inequality show that every $v$ with $\|v-u\|_2<d/2$ also lies outside $C$. Thus $C$ is closed. [given, F1, F4, construct, algebra]
lem-ip-bpdn-objectives-proper-closed-con.2.1: By [F5], $\operatorname{epi}g=C\times[0,\infty)$. If $(u,t)$ is outside this epigraph, either $u\notin C$ or $t<0$. In the first case step 1.3 supplies an open ball about $u$ disjoint from $C$, hence a product neighborhood disjoint from the epigraph; in the second case an interval about $t$ contained in $(-\infty,0)$ supplies such a product neighborhood. Therefore $\operatorname{epi}g$ is closed. Since $C$ is nonempty by step 1.3, $g$ is proper. If both endpoints lie in $C$, their convex combination lies in $C$ by step 1.3 and $g$ is zero there; if either endpoint has value $+\infty$ with positive coefficient, the convexity inequality has right side $+\infty$. Endpoint coefficients reduce to equality at the endpoint with coefficient one. Thus $g$ is convex, and [F2] proves that both functions have the asserted proper, closed, convex properties. [F2, F3, F5, step 1.3, construct, algebra] ∎

lem-fenchel-conjugate-is-proper-closed-c.1.1: Choose $x_0\in\operatorname{dom}f$ by [F3]. The affine minorant [F2] gives $\langle a,x\rangle-f(x)\le-b$ for every $x$ with finite $f(x)$, so $f^*(a)\le-b<+\infty$. The term at $x_0$ gives $f^*(a)\ge\langle a,x_0\rangle-f(x_0)>-\infty$. Thus $f^*$ is proper. [A1, F1, F2, F3, choose]
lem-fenchel-conjugate-is-proper-closed-c.1.2: If $n=0$, [F4] gives the singleton $\mathbb R^0=\{0\}$ and properness makes $f(0)$ finite, so $f^*(0)=-f(0)$ is proper, closed and convex directly. Hence assume $n\ge1$. For each $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$ and $s,s'\in\mathbb R^n$, [F5] gives $|\langle s,x\rangle-\langle s',x\rangle|\le\lVert s-s'\rVert_2\lVert x\rVert_2=d_2(s,s')\lVert x\rVert_2$. Thus $s\mapsto\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)$ is finite continuous affine. A pointwise supremum of these affine functions is convex: apply each affine function to $(1-\theta)s_0+\theta s_1$, bound by $(1-\theta)f^*(s_0)+\theta f^*(s_1)$, then take the supremum. [A1, F1, F4, F5, algebra]
lem-fenchel-conjugate-is-proper-closed-c.2.1: The epigraph of $f^*$ is the intersection, over $x\in\operatorname{dom}f$, of the closed half-spaces $$\{(s,t):t\ge\langle s,x\rangle-f(x)\}.$$ Each half-space is closed because its defining affine function is continuous by step 1.2, and any intersection of closed sets is closed. Hence $f^*$ is closed in the epigraph convention of [F3]. [A1, F1, F3, F4, F5, step 1.2, algebra] ∎

thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolven.2.1: By [F2], completing the square gives $$H(x)\ge b+\langle a,x\rangle+\frac{\|x-v\|_2^2}{2t}=b+\langle a,v\rangle-\frac t2\|a\|_2^2+\frac1{2t}\|x-(v-ta)\|_2^2.$$ Thus $H(x)\le c$ forces $x$ into a fixed-radius ball, so $S$ is bounded and hence compact by [F4]. The restriction $H|_S$ is real-valued; each weak sublevel set is the intersection of $S$ with the inverse image of $\operatorname{epi}H$ under $x\mapsto(x,r)$ for its level $r$, hence closed in $S$. By [F6] it is lower semicontinuous, so [F5] gives a minimizer on $S$. Every point outside $S$ has value greater than $c$, while the minimum on $S$ is at most $c$, so this minimizer is global. [F2, F4, F5, F6, step 1.2, algebra]
thm-proximal-operator-existence-resolven.2.2: The quadratic satisfies $\|\frac{x+y}{2}-v\|_2^2=\frac12\|x-v\|_2^2+\frac12\|y-v\|_2^2-\frac14\|x-y\|_2^2$. If two distinct points minimized $H$, convexity of $g$ and this identity would make their midpoint have strictly smaller value, a contradiction. Hence the global minimizer is unique, proving the singleton claim. [F1, step 1.2, algebra]

lem-ip-bpdn-minimizer-exists.1.1: Put $M_A=(\sum_{i=1}^m\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}^2)^{1/2}$. For $u,v\in\mathbb R^n$, rowwise Cauchy–Schwarz [F4] and finite-sum monotonicity [F5] give $\|A(u-v)\|_2^2=\sum_{i=1}^m\left(\sum_{j=1}^n A_{ij}(u_j-v_j)\right)^2\le M_A^2\|u-v\|_2^2.$ By [F6], $\|A(u-v)\|_2\le M_A\|u-v\|_2$. The reverse triangle inequality [F3] now gives $\big|\|Au-y\|_2-\|Av-y\|_2\big|\le\|A(u-v)\|_2\le M_A\|u-v\|_2.$ If $M_A=0$, the displayed bound gives $\|A(u-v)\|_2=0$ for every $u,v$; positive definiteness in [F3] gives $A(u-v)=0$, so the residual function is constant and nonemptiness gives $F=\mathbb R^n$. If $M_A>0$ and $z\notin F$, the positive gap $d=\|Az-y\|_2-\epsilon$ shows that every $u$ with $\|u-z\|_2<d/(2M_A)$ also lies outside $F$. Thus $F$ is closed. [given, F1, F2, F3, F4, F5, F6, construct, algebra]
lem-ip-bpdn-minimizer-exists.2.1: Fix one $z_0\in F$ and set $K=F\cap\{z:\|z\|_1\le\|z_0\|_1\}$. This set is nonempty because it contains $z_0$. If $\|z\|_1>\|z_0\|_1$, the positive gap $d=\|z\|_1-\|z_0\|_1$ and [F3] show that every $u$ with $\|u-z\|_2<d/(2\sqrt{n})$ still has $\|u\|_1>\|z_0\|_1$; the denominator is positive by [F9]. Thus the second factor is closed, and $K$ is closed by step 1.1. It is bounded since [F3] gives $\|z\|_2\le\|z\|_1\le\|z_0\|_1$ for every $z\in K$. By [F7], $K$ is compact. [given, F2, F3, F7, F8, F9, step 1.1, choose]
lem-ip-bpdn-minimizer-exists.3.1: The function $z\mapsto\|z\|_1$ is continuous by [F3], so [F7] gives a minimizer on the nonempty compact set $K$. Every feasible point outside $K$ has $\|z\|_1>\|z_0\|_1$, while the minimum on $K$ is at most $\|z_0\|_1$. Hence this minimum is global on $F$. The proof selects only one witness $z_0$ and uses the stated ZF compactness theorem; no choice axiom is used. [given, F3, F7, step 2.1, algebra] ∎

lem-ip-bpdn-dual-certificates.1.2: Let $z$ be any feasible vector and put $q=A^*p$. The condition $\|q\|_\infty\le1$ means $|q_j|\le1$ for every coordinate. Hence each term $|z_j|+q_jz_j$ is nonnegative, and [F7] gives $\|z\|_1+\langle q,z\rangle=\sum_j(|z_j|+q_jz_j)\ge0.$ By [F4], $\|z\|_1\ge-\langle p,Az\rangle$. Feasibility and [F6] give $|\langle p,Az-y\rangle|\le\epsilon\|p\|_2$, so $\|z\|_1\ge-\langle p,Az\rangle\ge-\langle p,y\rangle-\epsilon\|p\|_2.$ If $x$ is feasible and attains equality with the last quantity, it has objective no larger than any feasible $z$, proving the optimality certificate. [given, F3, F4, F5, F6, F7, algebra]
lem-ip-bpdn-dual-certificates.2.1: If $p\ne0$, $A^*p=0$, and $|\langle p,y\rangle|>\epsilon\|p\|_2$, then for every $z\in\mathbb R^n$, [F4] gives $|\langle p,Az-y\rangle|=|\langle A^*p,z\rangle-\langle p,y\rangle|=|\langle p,y\rangle|>\epsilon\|p\|_2.$ By [F6], this forces $\|Az-y\|_2>\epsilon$. Thus no $z$ is feasible, proving the infeasibility certificate. [given, F4, F6, F8, algebra] ∎

thm-knot-wirtinger-presentation-correctn.1.1: The input code has finite vertex, edge, segment and crossing lists, so each incidence check and each pairwise segment test is a finite loop; the exact determinant, rational intersection and endpoint-order operations terminate. A failed validation returns `invalid-input`. If validation succeeds, the one-component tracing follows the finite cyclic list of edges and paired half-edges from $a_0$, returns to $a_0$ after finitely many steps, and labels each maximal under-arc once. The crossing pass then visits the finite crossing list once, appends exactly the relator specified by the positive-normal source and target at each crossing, and returns the finite presentation. Thus the procedure terminates with one generator per under-arc and one relator per crossing, as claimed. If $c=0$, the explicit punctured-product model in [F1] gives its fundamental group as infinite cyclic on the positive meridian (the sphere factor is simply connected), while [F6]–[F8] identify the returned one-generator empty-relator presentation with the same free cyclic group. If $c>0$, [F1] and [F5] give the free meridian basis for the meridian region. [F1, F5, F6, F7, F8, F10, F11, given, construct, algebra]
thm-knot-wirtinger-presentation-correctn.2.1: Assume $c>0$ and add the crossing pieces in any fixed order. The ordered-intersection condition in [F1] makes the intersection at each attachment precisely its annular core. By [F3] and [F4], van Kampen kills the normal closure of that core's image; [F2] identifies this image with the relator emitted at that crossing. Repeating over the finite crossing set yields the quotient of the free meridian group by exactly the constructor's relator normal closure. [F1, F2, F3, F4, step 1.1, algebra]
thm-knot-wirtinger-presentation-correctn.3.1: By [F6] and [F7], the quotient in step 2.1 is the returned presentation group; [F8] identifies the quotient map with the homomorphism sending each symbol to its positive meridian. It is an isomorphism onto the group of the covered exterior by the pushout construction. [F3, F4, F6, F7, F8, step 2.1, algebra]
